title: Disputing the claim that uptown New Orleans musicians did not read music
summary: Jackson disagrees that uptown players could not read, citing Professor George Correa, the Humphrey family, Celestin and his own 1921 visit where he handed out parts.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Piron. He played with Piron, the fellas, see, long before I thought about playing. But we went to school together in the third and fourth grade. Then there was Humphrey, Willie Humphrey, Willie Humphrey. The reason I'm breaking up some of these fellas, Bill, while reading the book that you gave me, I noted in there, I think it was Dominic who said that the musicians downtown read and
the musicians in downtown didn't read.
I begged to differ with him. I'm going a little further back now, Bill, let's begin to come to me. Professor George Correa was a neighbor of mine.
Now I read something about George Correa in some other books about a year ago, another book that had been edited. And there was Professor Humphrey.
Yeah, sure, I know. And Roy did. And Roy did.

Roy read music. And so I don't see where they got the idea that Uptown the fellas didn't. Maybe Dominic was a little, we're good friends, but maybe a little precious because Dominic was from downtown, you see.
Well, I don't think Dominic, some other people told us that, like some people said that Bolden didn't read. Well maybe Bolden didn't.
There's a whole lot of them white musicians didn't read either.

See what I'm talking about? So I mean I lived right across the street from Professor George Correa, and when I lived on Upper Line Street I was only two blocks from the Humphreys, and Mrs. Humphrey, old man Humphrey's daughter, taught me in the fourth grade at Tarly Farm School. And she taught us a little music there. And so she knew music and evidently I think she must have gotten from her father. And Willie Humphrey today, if he's still living, he reads a lot of music. His brother Earl was a trombone player, then he has a younger brother, plays the drum, Pricy.
Well he's in the Eureka, the trumpet player, and he's the leader of the Eureka band, the brass band.

Well all right then. So they cannot tell me that the musicians didn't read because I begged to differ with them. Because when I went to New Orleans in 21 to visit, I brought some music down there and I did a little playing around there with Red A. Well Red A didn't do any of the French, or Morris French didn't read either. But some of the men, like Zip, some of the men didn't read because I passed out the parts. And they did read. But Red A had a good ear once they played something over. Well once or twice and they had it. So I used to sit in with those fellas at San Suzy Hall in 1921. I was just playing a fair myself at the time. But Morris French was supposed to be one of the top trombone players during that time. He was with Red A's band, see? And so I know that some of the music, it didn't make any difference what part of New Orleans the fella did.
No I don't think so either.
